notes.description:
Three days, and they are not a gentle introduction — a short VO2 session today, tempo with jammers tomorrow, then two and a half hours on Sunday with sprints late in the ride.

The point is to find out where you are before we start building. Ride them honestly and tell me if anything felt badly off.

Saturday is off. It is off every week.
notes.title: WEEK 0 — STRAIGHT IN

notes.description:
Six weeks to Mammoth Tuff, Saturday 19 September.

———

YOUR FULL GUIDE
{guide_url}

Sixteen sections covering zones, fuelling, recovery, kit, race week, race day, gravel skills, heat and altitude. There is a PDF on that page if you would rather keep a copy or print it.

Read sections 1 and 2 before Sunday. The rest keeps.

———

FIRST, THREE SETTINGS TO FIX
Your TrainingPeaks account has been dormant a while and is carrying old numbers that will argue with this plan until you change them.

1. Your birthday — TP has you at 19, which is where its wrong maximum heart rate comes from.
2. Heart rate — TP holds a threshold of 148 and a max of 200. Set them to 165 and 185, the numbers you gave me.
3. Power — TP holds an FTP from years back. Ignore the watts it shows you until after Wednesday of week one.

Settings > Zones for the last two. Ten minutes.

———

HOW THE WEEK WORKS
Sunday is the big day and everything protects it. Monday is a steady ride on legs that have not recovered — deliberate, and where durability comes from. Wednesday and Thursday carry the quality. Friday is aerobic volume. Saturday is off, as you asked.

If a week falls apart, protect Sunday and Wednesday and let the rest go.

———

READING THE WORKOUTS
Each one gives you power as a percentage, a zone, and an RPE. You ride on feel and heart rate, so RPE is your primary handle and the percentages become real numbers after Wednesday's test.

Your heart-rate bands, off a threshold of 165:
Recovery under 112 · Endurance 114-137 · Tempo 139-155 · Threshold 157-173 · Hard 175+

HR lags effort by a minute or two on climbs and drifts up late in long rides at the same effort. Both are normal. When HR and RPE disagree, trust RPE.

———

NEED THIS ADJUSTED?
Email me at gravelgodcoachingatgmail.com. Tell me what happened and what you want changed — a week that fell apart, a session that felt wrong, travel, illness, a day that no longer works. Adjusting a plan is normal and costs you nothing. Grinding through something that is not working costs you weeks.
notes.title: START HERE — Your Mammoth Tuff Plan

notes.description:
Wednesday is the session that matters: a 20-minute all-out FTP test. Everything downstream scales off the number it produces, so give it a real go.

Set the trainer to RESISTANCE or LEVEL mode, not ERG. In ERG it will hold you at the old, wrong number instead of letting you show what you can actually do.

The rest of the week: steady Monday, easy Tuesday, mixed climbs Thursday, aerobic Friday, and 3h15 Sunday with a 15-minute tempo block every hour.
notes.title: WEEK 1 — TEST WEEK

notes.description:
The mental side of this gets the same treatment as the physical: a few short things, practised until they are automatic. This is the first.

———

CENTERING YOUR BIOLOGY
Under stress your breathing goes shallow and fast, which tells your nervous system there is a threat, which makes you feel worse, which makes the breathing worse. You can break that loop from either end, and breathing is the end you control.

———

THE 6-2-7 FORMULA
Breathe in for 6, hold for 2, out for 7. The long exhale is the active ingredient — it is what drops your heart rate.

Do it for two minutes before a hard session, and again in the first ten minutes of a race when everything feels too fast. Practise it now, on easy days, so it is available when you need it. A technique you have never rehearsed will not show up on race day.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 1 — Breathing, And Why It Is First

notes.description:
Take your average power for the 20-minute effort and multiply it by 0.95. That is your FTP.

Put it into TrainingPeaks: Settings > Zones > Power. Every workout in the plan then shows real targets instead of percentages.

———

THEN SEND IT TO ME
Reply with the number and how the test felt — whether you paced it well, whether you had more at the end, whether you had to stop. That tells me as much as the number does, and it is the first point where I can adjust anything that is aimed wrong.

{coach_email}
notes.title: AFTER TODAY'S TEST — Send Me The Number

notes.description:
The first full build week. Wednesday is Float Sets — hard efforts with tempo in between rather than easy spinning, so your heart rate never fully comes down. Thursday is Mixed Climbing: seated grinding alternating with standing lifts, which is the shape of a real gravel climb.

Sunday is three hours of race-specific VO2 work — each effort opens with a 20-second sprint to simulate following an attack. That is the closest thing yet to what a gravel race actually does to you.

Start practising your race food on Sunday. Whatever you plan to eat at Mammoth, eat it then.
notes.title: WEEK 2 — BUILD

notes.description:
———

THE CHESS GAME
Somewhere in hour four your brain will offer you: "I can't hold this." "Everyone is stronger than me." "I should have trained more."

You do not have to argue with any of it. Arguing is playing the game. The move is to notice the thought, name it as a thought rather than a fact, and go back to what you were doing — the next ten miles, the next thing to eat.

———

PERFORMANCE STATEMENTS
Have two or three short phrases ready before race day. Not affirmations — instructions. Things like: "Smooth and steady." "Eat now." "Ride your own effort."

Short, specific, actionable. Write them down this week and use them on your long rides, so by 19 September they are a habit rather than something you are trying for the first time while suffering.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 2 — You Are Not Your Thoughts

notes.description:
Your gut is trainable and it needs the repetitions, so the target climbs with the long rides rather than appearing on race morning.

9 Aug — 45 g/hr
16 Aug — 55
23 Aug — 60
30 Aug — 65
6 Sep — 65-70 (race rate, on the five-hour rehearsal)
13 Sep — 60
Race day — 65-70

Sessions under 90 minutes are not on the ladder — eat what you like on those.

Where an individual workout quotes a different number, use the ladder. It is built for your body weight and for how long you will actually be out there.

———

WHAT THAT LOOKS LIKE
Roughly 25-35 g every 25-30 minutes, starting inside the first half hour. Set a timer. Read the labels rather than counting items — gels run anywhere from 20 to 40 g, and drink mixes vary as much, so "a gel every half hour" can quietly leave you well short.

Hunger is a lagging indicator. By the time you feel empty you are already an hour behind.

———

FLUID
Drink to thirst. 500-750 ml/hr is a starting estimate to adjust for heat and sweat rate, not a quota to hit. 500-1000 mg sodium per hour.

Do not force fluid beyond thirst across a long day. The simple check is that you should finish a shade lighter than you started, never heavier.
notes.title: FUELLING — The Ladder

notes.description:
Wednesday is Broken VO2 — three sets of 40/20s. Control the first two sets and only push the third if you genuinely feel good. Thursday is over-unders.

Sunday is the big one: 3h53 with high-cadence work, sprint sets, low-cadence blocks and a pyramid in the final hour. It is a long day with a lot in it — pace the early sets so the pyramid is still possible.

This is the last build week before your peak. If you are accumulating fatigue faster than you are absorbing it, this is the week to tell me.
notes.title: WEEK 3 — BUILD

notes.description:
You are through the hardest part of the build's first half. Worth an honest audit before the peak week:

· Are you finishing the Sunday rides, or surviving them?
· Is your sleep holding up?
· Are you hungry all the time, or has your appetite gone?
· Is anything hurting that was not hurting three weeks ago?
· Are you looking forward to riding, or dreading it?

Two or more of those pointing the wrong way and we should take something out now rather than in week five.

———

NEED THIS ADJUSTED?
Email me at gravelgodcoachingatgmail.com. Tell me what happened and what you want changed — a week that fell apart, a session that felt wrong, travel, illness, a day that no longer works. Adjusting a plan is normal and costs you nothing. Grinding through something that is not working costs you weeks.
notes.title: CHECK-IN — Two Weeks In. How Is It Landing?

notes.description:
Mid-September at Mammoth runs roughly 40-70°F: cold at the
start, warm by the middle of the day. The heat is not extreme, but two things about high-altitude sun catch people out.

———

THE SUN IS THE REAL ISSUE
At 8,000 feet there is a third less atmosphere filtering UV than at sea level. You will burn faster than the temperature suggests, and sunburn measurably raises how hard a given effort feels. Sunscreen before the start and again at an aid station, and do not skip it because the morning is cold.

———

THE SWING
A 30-degree swing between the start and the middle of the day means whatever you wear at 7am will be wrong by 11am. Plan for a layer you can lose and actually carry — arm warmers and a gilet that pack small beat a jacket you will not want to hang on to.

———

TRAINING FOR IT
If you get a genuinely hot week between now and the race, ride in it rather than moving indoors. Most heat adaptation arrives inside 7-10 exposures and it holds for a couple of weeks. Do it on easy days, never on a quality day, and back off if your heart rate climbs at an effort that normally sits lower.

Drink to thirst, and add sodium rather than volume when it is hot.
notes.title: HEAT AND SUN — Two Different Problems

notes.description:
The biggest week of the plan, and Sunday is the biggest day: 5h23. Race kit, race bike, race tyre pressure, race food, race start time if you can arrange it.

It is built like a race — high-cadence work early, sprint sets, then three long blocks alternating normal and low cadence, then two pyramids in the final hour when you are already tired. Nothing about race day should be new to you after this.

Everything after Sunday points at freshness. Do not add anything this week.
notes.title: WEEK 4 — PEAK

notes.description:
———

BUILD IT NOW
Think of three or four times you rode genuinely well. Not podiums necessarily — the day you held a wheel you did not expect to, the climb that went better than it should have, the ride you finished when you wanted to stop.

Write them down in detail. What you could see, what your legs felt like, what you told yourself.

———

WHY
Confidence is not a mood, it is evidence. When it deserts you at mile 50 you will not be able to conjure it, but you can recall it — and specific, sensory memories are far more usable than a general belief that you are fit.

Read them the night before the race. Run one of them in your head on the start line.

———

WHO YOU ARE ON THE BIKE
One more: finish the sentence "I am the kind of rider who ______" three times. How you describe yourself shapes what you attempt. If everything you write is about surviving, that is worth noticing before race day — you have done the work to say something better.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 3 — Your Highlight Reel

notes.description:
You will feel worse before you feel better this week. That is the taper working, and it is normal to feel flat and slightly anxious in the middle of it.

Volume drops hard. Wednesday is thirty-fifteens — high stimulus, low damage. Sunday is three hours of endurance with a six-second sprint every fifteen minutes, just to keep the legs lively.

Finish Sunday feeling like you could have done another hour. If you finish it tired, you overcooked it.
notes.title: WEEK 5 — RECOVERY & SHARPEN

notes.description:
While yesterday is still fresh, note:

· What you ate and when. Did you hit the target, or drift?
· What your stomach did in hours three to five.
· What chafed, rubbed, went numb or ached.
· What you ran out of.
· How the last hour felt, honestly.
· What you would change about the pacing.

Send it to me. Twelve days is enough to fix kit, fuelling and pacing — but only if we know what broke.

{coach_email}
notes.title: REHEARSAL DEBRIEF — Write It Down And Send It

notes.description:
Nothing you do this week adds fitness. Plenty could subtract it.

Tuesday is short and sharp — going hard, but not reaching for the last five percent. Wednesday is easy aerobic. Thursday is off. Friday is travel, bike check, and openers to prime the legs. Saturday you race.

Sleep is the training this week. Eat normally and a little more than feels necessary.
notes.title: WEEK 6 — RACE WEEK

notes.description:
———

WHICHEVER COURSE YOU ARE ON
The 67-mile route is roughly five hours and 3,500 feet of climbing. The 89 — the longer UCI qualifying option — is seven to eight hours and 7,500 feet. Worth checking which your entry says: for qualifying they are split by age, with the 89 for riders 19-49 and the 67 for 50 and over.

Your training does not change between them. Your pacing and the amount of food you carry do: longer course, more conservative first half, close to twice the total fuel.

———

ALTITUDE
The race sits between 7,880 and 8,100 feet the whole way. It is the defining feature of the event.

At any given effort your power and speed will be lower than at home and breathing will be harder from the gun. Heart rate is the unreliable one — it can sit higher than usual at easy paces and refuse to climb when you push late. Do not chase your familiar numbers up there. Ride to RPE.

If you already live and train at altitude you are largely covered. If you live near sea level, a week or more up there beforehand is best if practical; otherwise arriving close to the start is a reasonable compromise, since the first days at altitude are usually the roughest.

———

PACING
Start easier than feels right. At altitude an early overspend is not repaid later — it compounds. First third RPE 4-5, middle third 5-6, and spend what is left in the last third. People will come past you in the first hour. A good number of them come back.

———

WHEN IT GETS BAD
It will, somewhere. Break what remains into ten-mile pieces and ride the piece you are in. Eat something. Often it passes inside twenty minutes.

What is not a bad patch, and means stop and find a medic: chest pain, confusion, or a headache that keeps building.

———

FRIDAY NIGHT
Bottles mixed. Food in pockets and counted against where the aid stations actually are. Kit laid out. Tyres checked. Computer charged. Then stop.

———

WORTH RE-READING THIS WEEK
Sections 11 and 12 of your guide — Race Week and Race Day: {guide_url}

———

ANY LAST QUESTIONS
Send them this week rather than Friday night — gravelgodcoachingatgmail.com. Nothing is too small to ask about.
notes.title: RACE WEEK — Mammoth Tuff, Saturday 19 September

notes.description:
———

MUSIC
If music helps you, build the playlist this week rather than on the drive up. Be deliberate: something calm for the morning, something that lifts you for the last hour. What you listen to before a start genuinely shifts how you feel at it — pick accordingly rather than by accident.

———

THE NIGHT BEFORE
Read your highlight reel. Run through your performance statements. Then stop thinking about the race — the work is done and rehearsing it further only costs sleep.

———

ON THE LINE
Two minutes of 6-2-7 breathing. Everyone around you will look faster and more organised than you feel. They are not.

Your first job is to start easier than feels right. Everything after that is eating on time and riding your own effort.

You have done the work. Go and use it.
notes.title: GRAVEL GRIT 4 — The Last Three Days

notes.description:
Nothing today. Eat, drink, sleep.

If the legs feel stiff tomorrow, thirty minutes of easy spinning helps more than sitting still. Otherwise take the week easy and let it land.

When you have had a day to think about it, send me your race notes: what worked, what you would change, what surprised you, and what you want to do next. That is what the next plan gets built on.

{coach_email}

Four hard efforts with tempo in between instead of easy spinning. The floats are the whole point: your heart rate never comes back down, so the fourth effort starts from somewhere close to where the third finished. That is what a climb after a climb feels like.

4 x 4 minutes hard (RPE 8-9), and between each one 3 minutes at a firm tempo (RPE 6) rather than freewheeling. Do not stop pedalling in the floats — if you recover fully, the session has not worked.

workouts.description:
Four minutes just under your limit, then one minute clearly over it, three times without stopping. Twice. This trains the thing that actually loses races: clearing the accumulated burn while still working, instead of needing to sit up.

The unders are RPE 7 — firm and sustainable. The overs are RPE 9 and should hurt. Then you go straight back to the under, and it will feel much harder than it did the first time.

That is the session working. Five minutes easy between blocks. Do not let the unders drift down to make the overs easier.

Shorter and harder as it goes: four minutes, three, two, one, each one faster than the last. Your peak session of the plan, and the one that lifts the ceiling everything else sits under.

4 min (RPE 8) / 3 min (RPE 8-9) / 2 min (RPE 9) / 1 min (RPE 10), then after 3 easy a second pass at 4 min and 3 min. Three minutes easy between every effort.

The trap is starting the first four-minute too hard and having nothing left for the back half. Pace the opener, empty the one-minute, then hang on for the last two.

workouts.description:
A six-second full-gas burst every minute on top of a tempo floor, for twelve minutes, three times. Washboard, punchy risers, closing a gap when the wheel in front goes — that is what this is. Big neuromuscular effect, surprisingly little damage.

Hold RPE 6-7 between bursts and do not let it sag, then hit each burst genuinely hard for six seconds and settle straight back. Out of the saddle for the bursts is fine.

Five minutes easy between blocks. The floor between bursts is the session; the bursts are the seasoning.

Three sets of nine very short, very hard efforts with barely any rest. High stimulus, low damage — it keeps the top end awake through the taper without leaving a mark on your legs for Saturday.

9 x (30 seconds hard / 15 seconds easy), three times through, with 4 minutes easy between sets. RPE 9 on the efforts and high cadence — spin them, do not grind them.

workouts.description:
WARM-UP:
• 10min easy spin building into the zone, 56-75% FTP (Z2).

MAIN SET:
• Endurance riding for the rest of the ride at 56-75% FTP (Z2); every 15min, one 6sec sprint/acceleration at 250-350% FTP, alternating seated and standing.
• Don't let cadence get bogged down between efforts — keep it lively.

COOL-DOWN:
• 5min easy spin, 40-50% FTP.

EXECUTION:
• Float through the bottom to the top of the zone. The sprints are just neuromuscular wake-up calls — snap up to speed, then settle right back into endurance pace.

NUTRITION: 60g carbs/hr — six days out, last long ride, hold the race pattern.
HYDRATION: 500-750ml/hr with electrolytes.

workouts.title: Openers v1.1

workouts.description:
Race day. You have done the work.

HOW LONG YOUR DAY IS. On the 67-mile course, expect somewhere around five hours. On the 89 — the longer UCI qualifying route — expect seven to eight, with 7,500 feet of climbing instead of 3,500. The pacing below matters more on the longer one, not less. This calendar entry is set to five hours; ignore that number if you are riding the 89.

PACING. The first hour will feel absurdly easy and you must let it. At 8,000 feet the cost of going too hard early is not paid back — it compounds. Ride the first third at RPE 4-5, the middle third at RPE 5-6, and only spend what is left in the last third. On the 89 that first third is nearly three hours of riding well within yourself. Do it anyway.

CLIMBS. Ride them at your effort, not the group's. People will come past you early. A good number of them come back.

HR. At altitude heart rate stops being a reliable guide — it can read high early, refuse to climb when you push late, and drift through the day regardless. Do not pace off it. Ride to RPE and look at HR afterwards.

FUEL. Same rate either way, 65-70 g carbs/hr — but the longer course means carrying or resupplying close to twice the total. Count it out the night before against where the aid stations actually are.

WHEN IT GETS BAD. It will, somewhere. Break the remaining distance into ten-mile pieces and ride the piece you are in. Eat something. Often it passes within twenty minutes or so. What is not a bad patch: chest pain, confusion, or a headache that keeps building — those mean stop and find a medic.

HEART RATE (you ride on feel and HR, so these are your real handles):
Recovery under 112 bpm · Endurance 114-137 bpm · Tempo 139-155 bpm · Threshold 157-173 bpm · Hard 175 bpm and above
Off your threshold HR of 165. HR lags effort by a minute or two on climbs and drifts up late in long rides at the same effort — that drift is normal. When HR and RPE disagree, trust RPE.
Note: your TrainingPeaks account still holds old threshold settings — use the bands above, not the zones TP displays, until you have updated them (see the START HERE note).

FUEL: 65-70 g carbs/hr — roughly 29-39 g every 25-30 minutes, starting inside the first 30 minutes. Check the label; gels, bars and drink mixes differ enormously. Drink to thirst, around 500-750 ml/hr as a starting estimate, adjusted for heat and how much you are sweating. 500-1000 mg sodium/hr. Do not force fluid beyond thirst — finishing heavier than you started is the one thing to avoid.
